intuition: Preorder tells us which node to create next. Inorder tells us when a left part has finished and a right part should begin. Keep unfinished ancestors on a stack. Attach new nodes on the left until the stack matches the next inorder value, then remove the finished ancestors.

Preorder tells us which node is introduced next; inorder tells us which left subtrees have already finished. Keep an ancestor stack and a cursor into inorder. If the stack top has not reached the cursor, a new node belongs on its left. When values match, pop completed roots until locating the ancestor whose right subtree begins next.
The uniqueness promise makes these matches unambiguous, and an explicit stack avoids deep recursive calls while constructing the actual node objects.

The stack is the active ancestor chain of preorder construction. Before an inorder match, preorder nodes belong to the top node's unbuilt left subtree. Matching and popping advances past fully built left subtrees and their roots; the last popped ancestor is exactly the root whose right subtree comes next. Valid distinct traversals make each attachment unique.
Each node is pushed and popped once; the stack is an ancestor path.

steps: Create root 3; inorder currently expects 9, so the next preorder value 9 attaches as 3.left.
Before introducing 20, pop 9 because inorder reaches it, then pop 3 because inorder reaches it too.
Attach 20 to the last popped node’s right, making 3.right=20.
Inorder now expects 15; attach preorder value 15 as 20.left.
Pop 15 and then 20 when inorder reaches them, and attach 7 as 20.right.

concept.question: How do arrival order and left-to-right order reveal the same tree?

concept.correctness: Preorder supplies each subtree root before any of its descendants. Inorder tells when the left descendants and that root have been fully visited. The stack preserves the unfinished ancestor chain, so closing matching ancestors identifies exactly where the next right subtree belongs. With distinct values, these traversal positions uniquely determine the reconstructed tree.
